items.title: 61520_Teddy Edwards oral history interview
items.q: That's my grandfather on my mother's side, Henry Carson Reed. And they used to call him Professor, and Fess for short

ctx.x: That's my grandfather on my mother's side, Henry Carson Reed. And they used to call him Professor, and Fess for short -- so everybody knew him around home as Fess Reed. Actually, he was one of the early upright bass players, string bass players in Jazz bands.

items.title: 61520_Teddy Edwards oral history interview
items.q: I first saw Earl Fatha Hines when he came to Detroit, and I heard Billy Eckstine with him at the time

ctx.x: Oh, I'll get to that in a few minutes. Okay? [LAUGHS]

There was plenty of good listening around the city during that period. I remember going down to the Michigan Theatre. That's where I first heard Frank Sinatra with the Tommy Dorsey Orchestra. That was a real treat. And Timmy Rogers was on the bill, the comedian and musician; he was on the bill. That was an exciting show.

items.title: 61520_Teddy Edwards oral history interview
items.q: I had an opportunity to hear a lot of great bands, like Earl Hines... But one of my favorites was Earl Fatha Hines.

ctx.x: Yeah. It was on North Farris Street in Jackson. That was the big dance hall where all the bands played. I had an opportunity to hear a lot of great bands, like Earl Hines, Tiny Bradshaw, (?), they had Joe Robicheaux -- a lot of different bands that came through there. I heard Andy Kirk's band, and also Erskine Hawkins. And we also had another ballroom called the Savoy Ballroom, and I used to play there on some matinees that they would have at the Savoy with Paul Gayten's little group. And we also used to…

items.title: 61520_Teddy Edwards oral history interview
items.q: I also had heard Billie Holiday for my first time at the Paradise Theatre, and I heard Sarah Vaughan the first time at the Paradise Theatre. The first time she came to Detroit with Fatha Hines...

ctx.x: I also had heard Billie Holiday for my first time at the Paradise Theatre, and I heard Sarah Vaughan the first time at the Paradise Theatre. The first time she came to Detroit with Fatha Hines, they were playing two pianos back to back, two pianos on the stage, and she was playing and he was playing -- there were two white pianos sitting out in front of the band. And they really used to do show business(?) up. It was really something.

One of my favorite ladies that I saw at the Graystone Ballroom was Miss Lil Green. She had the big hits out, "In The Dark" and "I Want To Copyright Your Love" and all those things. And she'd just stand up there and just let it just roll out, you know. She didn't do any body movements at all. She'd just stand up there and let the sounds come out, you know.
